title: Mikasa: lunch aboard the flagship and the problem of supply
dek: During the blockade of Port Arthur, 156 people aboard Mikasa suffered food poisoning. The shortage of food supply ships was recognised as a problem of that war, yet the fleet’s first dedicated food supply ship did not enter service until 1924.

sections.title: The flagship off Port Arthur
paragraphs: During the Russo-Japanese War, the battleship Mikasa took part in blockade operations off Port Arthur. She was an armoured Japanese warship and the flagship of the Combined Fleet—the ship carrying its commander. The Russian squadron was in its base; the Japanese ships operated outside it. They too needed an anchorage where they could undergo maintenance and replenish supplies. From 10 May 1904, Mikasa was undergoing maintenance at a forward base among the islands south of China’s Liaodong Peninsula.
The ship was still there on 30 May. Japanese historian Akinori Ishihara described that day’s lunch and the food poisoning that followed in his study of naval supply.

Rice and barley, soup with dried radish and tea were on the breakfast menu. More rice for lunch, with stewed canned salmon and seaweed, pickles and barley tea. For dinner, hardtack and roast beef with potatoes. At an anchorage where fresh food was scarce, Ishihara considers this a fairly ordinary menu.

sections.title: After lunch
paragraphs: The canned salmon had spoiled: its storage life had been exceeded. After lunch, 156 people aboard Mikasa fell ill. This happened on the flagship, at its own forward base, and the cause was food from the ship’s menu.

Food poisoning also occurred aboard other Japanese ships in May and June. Among the reported causes were canned goods, fried tofu (soybean curd) and mouldy bread; sometimes the offending food could not be identified. Aboard Mikasa, efforts were made to serve food that had been cooked: stewed, fried or boiled. The crew had to eat every day, despite all the difficulties of delivery and storage.

sections.title: From transport ship to the crew’s meal
paragraphs: At the start of the war, two auxiliary vessels, Matsuyama Maru and Fukuoka Maru, were prepared to supply food. Deliveries to the forward forces were planned roughly every six days. But the warships often operated in dispersed groups, and two supply vessels proved too few. From August 1904, Kotohira Maru and other ships were brought into this work.

The additional ships helped with transport, but they lacked enough equipment to preserve the food. They could not carry sufficient provisions. Even the few days’ voyage from the Japanese naval base at Sasebo to a forward base made it difficult to keep bread, vegetables, meat and fish fresh. Refrigeration technology already existed, but its installation aboard ships was only beginning.

The shortage of food supply vessels was recognised as one of the weaknesses of supply during the Russo-Japanese War. The auxiliary transports of 1904, however, were not yet the dedicated fleet food supply ships that appeared later. The first such ship in the Japanese navy, Mamiya, entered service in 1924. The second, Irako, followed on 5 December 1941. Ishihara argues that, against the backdrop of the Japanese fleet’s victory at Tsushima in 1905, the supply shortcomings exposed by the war were not adequately reflected in subsequent naval policy.

Feeding the crew during battle called for a different arrangement. On 27 May 1905, the first day of the Battle of Tsushima, hardtack and a drink made from kudzu starch were kept ready on Mikasa’s upper, middle and lower decks. Sailors could eat and drink as needed. Rice balls were handed out for dinner at five in the afternoon.
Regular meal arrangements resumed at eight that evening, when fighting paused for the night. The seriously wounded received special food: eggs, condensed milk and porridge.

limitations: The lunch and number of people taken ill are described in Ishihara’s 2024 study. The original medical volume has not been checked separately; 156 counts people taken ill, not deaths. No causal link has been established between the spoilage of this batch of canned salmon and the shortage of ships.

The dates for Mamiya and Irako refer to dedicated fleet food supply ships. Auxiliary vessels were already supplying food in 1904. The assessment of how the navy absorbed the war’s lessons is Ishihara’s.

title: Who could borrow in Dairen?
dek: A grain merchant could borrow against a railway consignment note; an established business client might need only a telephone call. How Chinese cash houses connected trade, savings and bank credit.
perspective: From bank clerk Sun Yaoting’s memoir and Guo Xipu and Sun’s account of Dalian’s cash houses

sections.title: A borrower who could help his bank
paragraphs: In Dairen in the 1920s and 1930s—the name of Dalian under Japanese rule—a large grain merchant might not only borrow from a bank but also come to its aid with money. Bank clerk Sun Yaoting named two such firms: Xingji, managed by Xin Bofen, and Yifahe, managed by Wang Xinzhai. They were major borrowers from banks and private cash houses. When necessary, the same trading firms supported their creditors when they ran short of funds for day-to-day payments.

Sun had worked in banking since 1930, including at the joint Japanese-Chinese Longkou Bank. These credit relationships rested on a particular business: grain trading and oil milling. Soybeans and gaoliang, or sorghum, came into the port; traders needed money while their goods were in transit. In another account of Dalian finance, Sun and Guo Xipu described a convenient form of security for a merchant: buy grain, hand the railway consignment note to a bank and obtain cash against it. In their judgement, a bank was more willing to accept a document covering grain in transit than a mortgage on property.

Such a loan was tied to a specific cargo and transaction. Another borrower needed guarantees of repayment of his own. Sun recalled that an ordinary resident found it hard to obtain a loan without adequate security. But between a large foreign bank and a private moneylender there was another option: a qianzhuang, or cash house.

sections.title: Property for the bank, trust for the client
paragraphs: Qianzhuang accepted deposits, made loans, exchanged money and transferred it to other cities. They were not pawnshops: their business extended beyond objects brought in as collateral. In the 1920s and early 1930s, they chiefly served Chinese commercial and industrial firms. According to Sun and Guo, a small business owner often preferred to pay them more rather than seek a loan from a foreign bank, with its complicated procedures and difficult access.

Cash houses had creditors of their own. They would generally mortgage property to a bank and arrange an overdraft—the right to draw more money from a current account than it held. Their own funds were insufficient: merchants left deposits for only short periods, and deposits from other residents were few. When incoming and outgoing payments did not balance, bank support was needed.

A cash house, in turn, might lend to a trusted client after a telephone call. There was no single interest rate or set of terms for everyone: the borrower’s standing mattered, as did the availability of money in the market. Sun gives one example of the cost of a short-term loan: two jiao, or two-tenths of a yuan, charged daily for every thousand yuan borrowed. He does not identify the lender or the length of the loan; treating this as the city’s average rate would be misleading.

sections.title: Where the money came from
paragraphs: In a table of cash houses for 1931, the entry for Yifahe lists Wang Xinzhai, capital of 300,000 yuan in banknotes and an opening date of 1923. Nearby are establishments with capital of only five thousand. But the amounts are recorded in different kinds of money: silver, “gold” banknotes, and large and small silver monetary units. They cannot be added together as though every yuan were the same.

The reputation of an owner and his shareholders brought in depositors, whose deposits made lending possible. Connections often grew around a shared place of origin. Businesspeople from Shandong were important clients of cash houses run by people from that province. Yifahe belonged to the influential group from Laoting in Hebei. Yet Sun qualified this: shared interests mattered as well as a shared home, and the groups’ membership could change.

There was also a more entertaining way to attract residents’ savings. Sun describes Wanguo Chuxu Hui, a savings scheme with a prize draw: pay in three yuan each month for a chance at the year-end top prize of 30,000. A printer at the Taidong Ribao newspaper won it once. Sun left neither the winner’s name nor the year, but remembered the scheme’s promotional success: these deposits began to spread among Chinese banks. Many small payments pooled money for banking operations.

sections.title: A consignment note could lead to the exchange
paragraphs: Grain cargoes connected the bank’s cash desk to the railway, but did not guarantee uneventful trading. Sun and Guo recalled that well-funded cash houses acting as agents could obtain cash against consignment notes and then take that money to the currency exchange. There, transactions involved not only cash currency but also contracts for future delivery. In their account, some participants grew rich quickly while others were ruined. Having security did not mean that a borrower would use the money only for the next consignment of grain.

Merchants and financiers also defended the system of payments they knew. When the Japanese authorities tried to replace the silver basis of currency circulation with a gold basis, representatives of cash houses, grain firms and oil mills submitted a joint petition. Sun recalled appeals to the Kwantung authorities and a delegation’s journey to Tokyo. He did not give the year. Even Japanese banks were divided: the Yokohama Specie Bank, which issued silver banknotes, also opposed abolishing the silver system.

sections.title: When a telephone call was no longer enough
paragraphs: In Sun’s account, the dispute ended with permission to use both systems, but Chinese financiers had to report their operations every month. They then strengthened their connections around a shared table: bank managers invited representatives of the chamber of commerce to weekly lunches at the Yamato Hotel. The gatherings were called Suiyokai, the Wednesday Society. Discussing business and supporting one another was a practical necessity.

War gradually narrowed this network’s scope. Sun and Guo’s account says that controls on grain undermined the business of trading agents, while the cash houses’ overseas transfers ceased. Its description of wartime restrictions gives the thresholds at which prior permission from the Japanese administration was required: industrial loans of 100,000 yuan or more, commercial loans of 50,000 or more, and overdrafts of 30,000 or more. By 1944, according to the account, only eight Chinese cash houses remained in Dalian.

Access to money had once begun with a grain consignment note, a shareholder’s reputation or a call to a familiar creditor. Now permits, reports and trade restrictions increasingly governed those relationships. A firm once able to help its bank depended on more than its goods and its depositors’ trust: the very transactions on which its credit rested could be closed to it.

limitations: These are retrospective accounts by participants in financial life, recorded and edited by Huang Benren. The first article was read in full, on pages 49–62 of the library PDF; the second on printed pages 91–106 (PDF pages 93–108). Sun contributes to both accounts, so they are not treated as two wholly independent testimonies.

Amounts and terms are given only as described in these accounts. Individual loan contracts, the named firms’ accounts and original Japanese regulations have not been checked. The two-jiao rate has not been converted into an annual rate; the currency issue used in that example is unspecified. Cash-house capital recorded in different currencies is not added together.

The first account omits the exact year of the dispute over the gold and silver systems. Its mistaken generalisations about Russian money and the continuity of banks are not adopted. The name, manager and credit connections of Yifahe do not establish that every similarly named firm was the same legal entity.
